Water gas is CO + H₂, so the problem is to get rid of the CO without losing the H₂.
The answer is the water-gas shift reaction. Pass the mixture with steam over a catalyst
(iron chromate at about 673 K):
CO + H₂O ⇒ CO₂ + H₂
Notice this does two useful things at once — it converts the unwanted CO into CO₂, and it
generates a further mole of H₂ from the steam.
CO₂ is then scrubbed out by passing the gas through water under pressure or through alkali,
because CO₂ is acidic and H₂ is not.
(B) is wrong because fractional separation on density is not how it is done industrially;
(C) diffusion and (D) occlusion on palladium are laboratory purifications, not the manufacture.
∴ CO is oxidised to CO₂ with steam over a catalyst, and the CO₂ is absorbed in alkali.

Plaster of Paris is made by heating gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O, to about 393 K (120 °C).
At that temperature it loses three quarters of its water of crystallisation:
2CaSO₄·2H₂O ⇒ 2CaSO₄·½H₂O + 3H₂O
So two formula units share one water molecule, giving the hemihydrate CaSO₄·½H₂O.
It is also written (CaSO₄)₂·H₂O, which is the same thing.
Adding water reverses the step and it sets back to gypsum — that is why it is used for casts.
Heating beyond 393 K gives dead burnt plaster, anhydrous CaSO₄ (D), which will not set.
∴ CaSO₄·½H₂O.

Borax is sodium tetraborate decahydrate, Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O.
In water it hydrolyses to give a buffer of boric acid and the metaborate ion, which is why
borax solution is alkaline.
Adding a strong mineral acid supplies H⁺, which drives the hydrolysis to completion:
Na₂B₄O₇ + 2HCl + 5H₂O ⇒ 2NaCl + 4H₃BO₃
The product H₃BO₃ is orthoboric acid, which crystallises out as white flakes.
Metaboric acid HBO₂ (C) and pyroboric acid H₂B₄O₇ (D) are formed by *heating* orthoboric acid
and driving water off, not by this reaction.
∴ orthoboric acid.

Sort each pair by what differs between them.
(A) n-Butane and isobutane are both C₄H₁₀ and both alkanes; only the branching differs,
so they are chain isomers, not functional isomers.
(B) Dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃) and ethanol (C₂H₅OH) are both C₂H₆O but one is an ether and the
other an alcohol — different functional groups, so they are functional isomers, not chain isomers.
(D) Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) and methyl methanoate (HCOOCH₃) are both C₂H₄O₂, an acid and an
ester — again functional isomers, not position isomers.
(C) Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are both C₃H₈O, both alcohols, same skeleton; only the position
of the –OH differs, C1 against C2. That is exactly the definition of position isomerism ✓
∴ statement (C) is correct.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|15||0|0:
Homolytic fission splits a bond evenly, one electron to each fragment, giving free radicals.
It needs a non-polar bond and an input of energy such as UV light, heat or a peroxide.
(A) Alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl chloride is nucleophilic substitution: OH⁻ attacks and Cl⁻ leaves
with both electrons — heterolytic.
(B) Addition of HBr across a double bond proceeds through H⁺ and a carbocation — heterolytic.
(D) Nitration of benzene uses the electrophile NO₂⁺, generated heterolytically — heterolytic.
(C) Chlorination of methane is initiated by UV light splitting Cl₂ into two chlorine atoms:
Cl–Cl ⇒ 2Cl• , one electron each. The chain then runs through CH₃• radicals ✓
∴ free radical chlorination of methane.

This is Kolbe's electrolytic method.
Electrolyse a concentrated aqueous solution of the sodium or potassium salt of a carboxylic acid.
At the anode the carboxylate ion loses an electron and then loses CO₂:
2RCOO⁻ ⇒ 2RCOO• + 2e⁻ ⇒ 2R• + 2CO₂
The two alkyl radicals couple:
2R• ⇒ R–R
So CH₃COO⁻ gives ethane, C₂H₆. Hydrogen is released at the cathode.
Note the alkane produced has twice the alkyl carbons, so this route only gives alkanes with an
even number of carbons from a single acid.
∴ the solution is subjected to electrolysis.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|17||0|0.s:
Photochemical smog forms in warm, dry, sunny cities from NO₂ and unburnt hydrocarbons.
Sunlight splits NO₂ into NO and an oxygen atom; that atom makes ozone, and ozone then reacts
with the hydrocarbons to make a series of irritants.
So its usual components are ozone (A), nitric oxide, acrolein (B), formaldehyde and
peroxyacetyl nitrate, PAN (C). These are oxidising, which is why it is called oxidising smog.
Chlorofluorocarbons are different in kind: they are unreactive at ground level, which is exactly
why they survive to drift into the stratosphere, where UV frees chlorine atoms that destroy ozone.
CFCs are the cause of ozone *depletion* high up, not a component of smog at street level.
∴ chlorofluorocarbons.
